segments: The following are general SOPS CLI examples; supported subcommands and argument placement depend on the installed version. Private-key read permissions and machine configuration determine whether administrator privileges are needed.
Subcommand overview
Editing plaintext: the core workflow
Method 1: sops edit (recommended, standard workflow)

It automatically decrypts → opens $EDITOR to edit plaintext → automatically encrypts and writes back after saving. You never handle the ciphertext directly, and there is no need to manually decrypt, edit, and encrypt.

Editing permissions
Administrators should first confirm the decryption identity and file write permissions. A dedicated user age identity avoids relying on the system host key for everyday editing. Do not put private keys in the repository or command arguments.
Method 2: edit in a restricted temporary file, then encrypt

Delete temporary plaintext
Use a randomly named private directory and 0700/0600 permissions for temporary files, set an exit cleanup hook, and prevent leaks through editor backups, swap files, and logs. Deletion does not guarantee secure erasure from the storage medium; choose an appropriately protected memory filesystem when needed. If encryption fails, do not overwrite the original ciphertext.
Method 3: set/unset (change one key without editing the entire file)
Encryption, decryption, and inspection
Key and recipient management

Remove a recipient: remove that key from .sops.yaml, then run sops updatekeys.
Rotate the data key (generate a new AES key and re-encrypt; existing recipients remain valid):

A safe key-change workflow Add the new recipient first (keep both as a safeguard) → verify that the new key can decrypt → remove the old recipient only after confirming stability. During the transition, rollback is possible if you retain the old ciphertext, old keys, and a working system recovery path. See the sops migration guide for the full process.
Understanding .sops.yaml
.sops.yaml is the sops client configuration file. It determines which public key encrypts which file. A general example follows (placeholders are not valid keys):
Field-by-field meaning:
Field
Meaning
A helper area for storing YAML anchors, not an independent SOPS authorization field
YAML anchor: assigns a label to a public-key string
An array of encryption rules, each matching certain files
A path regular expression determining which files a rule applies to
Key groups; within a group, any one identity can usually obtain the group’s share, while the Shamir threshold governs recovery across groups
YAML alias: resolves to the full public key

Multiple secrets files: creation_rules is an array, so you can add rules matching different files. Filenames are arbitrary as long as path_regex matches. Declare the runtime mapping in host/sops.nix using sopsFile:

The roles of .sops.yaml and host/sops.nix .sops.yaml controls which public key is used during encryption (CLI side); host/sops.nix controls which secret is taken from which file during decryption (runtime side). Their recipient and private key must match.
Regex vs. glob: * is a repetition operator, not a wildcard
In a regular expression (regex), * means repeat the preceding character, rather than the shell glob meaning of “match anything”:
YAML’s & / * are not pointers

&name (anchor) and *name (alias) are YAML declarations/references, not memory pointers. They express an anchor/alias relationship between YAML nodes: *server-key refers to the previously defined public-key node during parsing. Their purpose is to define once, reference many times, so a change needs to be made only at the & definition. “Variable-like” is a better analogy than “pointer.”
The layers behind the syntax
.sops.yaml has two layers of logic:
Layer
Defined by
Examples
Format layer (YAML syntax)
The YAML specification
&anchor, *alias, indentation, lists, and key-value pairs
Semantic layer (configuration fields)
Defined by sops
Anchors and aliases are YAML features; sops merely uses them. Fields such as path_regex are where sops-specific logic begins. This distinction applies to any tool that uses YAML for configuration.
How .sops.yaml is located: check the working directory and explicit configuration

By default, the current upstream CLI searches upward for configuration from the process’s current directory, . (configuration-path environment variables may also affect this), not from the target file’s directory. When invoking it across directories, run it from the repository root or specify the configuration explicitly with --config /path/to/config-repo/.sops.yaml. path_regex interprets the target path relative to the configuration file’s directory. When re-encrypting a temporary file, use --filename-override to specify the intended repository filename so the rules match.
The roles of .sops.yaml and sopsFile in sops.nix
In sops.nix: sopsFile
Who reads it
The sops-nix module
What it controls
Encryption/recipient-update rules and CLI storage options
Which source to decrypt at runtime and which secret to export
When it is needed
Creating ciphertext, updating authorization, and similar operations
Deploying secrets during system activation

SopsFile does not determine the recipient used for CLI encryption. Existing ciphertext carries key-wrapping metadata, so decryption itself does not depend on creation_rules. However, .sops.yaml can also define storage or editing options, so it cannot be described as being read at only two points.
Quick reference for NixOS

Command-line decryption and sops-nix runtime decryption use different entry points. sops-nix imports SSH keys through age.sshKeyPaths, whereas the SOPS CLI should explicitly use a readable age identity. --age takes an encryption recipient; a private-key file or process-substitution path cannot be supplied there in place of a decryption identity.

This is only an executable example; it was not run on the current machine. If other default age identities exist, disable those additional identities in an isolated, controlled environment before testing the target private key, to avoid a false positive.

The JSON value passed to set can enter shell history or process arguments; the example uses only non-secret strings. For real values, prefer sops edit or a controlled file/standard-input interface supported by the current version. sops -d -i turns the original repository file into plaintext and should generally be avoided. If used by mistake, stop committing and restore protected ciphertext. filestatus checks the encryption status recorded in the format; it does not prove that there have been no leaks, that decryption works, or that runtime deployment succeeded.
